title: Welcoming guests
hook: hospitality from Abraham's tent onward (Genesis 18): water, bread, and running to meet the stranger

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: a restful corner. Martha served, Mary sat, and one thing was needful. Today the door opens, and someone else comes in.

The heat of the day, a tent door, an old man sitting in it. Genesis 18: "he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day; And he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door". Abraham, in the heat, runs. He bows, and offers a little water to wash their feet, a rest under the tree, a morsel of bread. Then he hurries to Sarah: "Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth." He runs to the herd for a calf, brings butter and milk, and stands by them under the tree while they eat.
screen: `THE HEAT OF THE DAY, A TENT DOOR.` → `HE RAN TO MEET THEM.` → `CAKES UPON THE HEARTH.`

segments.voice: Smell the bread on the hearth; feel cool water on dusty feet. The story is all senses, and the guests turn out to be messengers of God. Jewish teaching made a commandment of what Abraham did: hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests. The Talmud draws a bold line from this chapter. It opens with the LORD appearing to Abraham, and then Abraham turns and runs to the strangers, so the rabbis say that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence. The Letter to the Hebrews, in the New Testament, looks back at the same tent: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." And the Qur'an tells of Abraham's guests and the calf he brought them too. In each of these tellings, the stranger at the door might be heaven's messenger. A welcome isn't the décor. It's the water, the bread, and staying by them while they eat.
screen: `A COMMANDMENT: BRING IN GUESTS.` · `GREATER THAN THE DIVINE PRESENCE.` · `ANGELS UNAWARES.` · `WATER, BREAD, AND STAYING BY THEM.` · then, large: `ABRAHAM'S TENT.`

segments.voice: Get up and walk, at an easy pace, to the door of the room you're in. Stand in the doorway for a breath or two, the way Abraham sat in his tent door, looking out. Then come back, sit, and let one person come to mind whom you could invite in, to your table or just your doorstep.
Welcoming guests: water, bread, and running to the door. Jews call it hachnasat orchim, and it begins at Abraham's tent.
The line to keep: Abraham's tent, where an old man ran out in the heat to meet strangers. The door's open.
